title: Judo: the Kodokan and throwing techniques
note: Jigoro Kano founded Kodokan judo in 1882 from older jujutsu schools. The Kodokan classifies 100 techniques: 68 nage-waza (throws) and 32 katame-waza (grappling). Throws split into tachi-waza, standing throws by hand, hip, or foot and leg, and sutemi-waza, sacrifice throws in which tori goes to the mat.

read.title: How the Kodokan sorts its throws
text: When Jigoro Kano opened the Kodokan in Tokyo in 1882, he drew on the jujutsu he had mastered, chiefly Tenjin Shin'yo-ryu and Kito-ryu, and reorganized it around principles that could be practiced safely at full effort. The name judo means the gentle way, not because it is soft, but because it yields to and redirects force.

The Kodokan's modern classification lists 100 techniques. Sixty-eight are nage-waza, throws, and thirty-two are katame-waza, grappling techniques. Throws are divided by how tori stays or falls. In tachi-waza, standing techniques, tori stays on the feet and throws mainly with the hands (te-waza), the hips (koshi-waza), or the feet and legs (ashi-waza). In sutemi-waza, sacrifice techniques, tori deliberately drops to the mat, either onto the back (ma-sutemi-waza) or onto the side (yoko-sutemi-waza).

So seoi-nage, the shoulder throw, is a hand technique; o-goshi, the major hip throw, is a hip technique; o-soto-gari, the major outer reap, is a leg technique; and tomoe-nage, the circle throw, in which tori falls back and lifts uke over with a foot, is a rear sacrifice.
